The straw that broke the camel's back?

User Interface.

Arch Linux: i3 WM

Distro: I wanted to get away from pre-managed installation wizards and configuration files. I appreciate the benefits and ease of use that installation managers provide, Pacman itself is pretty self-managed to a point. But there are still some things you just need to get directly involved with on Arch and I needed that again in my user experience. Additionally Arch is consistently the most up-to-date stable environment.

As accurately described in IRC, Arch Linux is the hot buns fresh out of the oven - not to be confused with the molten-lava buns still cooking in it.

WM: I can't express enough how much I love i3. Once you acclimate to the use of window tiling it becomes one of the most adaptive and productive window managers I've ever used. It isn't pretty with beveled edges, candy-colored title bars, and screen transitions - it is all the utility of a terminal-loving keyboard jockey with the benefit of graphical windows.

Additionally Arch is consistently the most up-to-date stable environment.

Typically a "rolling release" distro is less stable than one that has a versioned release cycle because there's maintainer effort that goes into the release to ensure it's stable. Arch and Gentoo are both "rolling release" distros. Neither are known for their stability.

Basically, use Arch if you love having the latest-and-greatest all the time, but don't claim that update X won't break package Y, and not provide you a way to undo the package you just installed.

Er, you can rollback packages, if that's what you meant. If you REALLY fucked things up you might need to do it from a livecd, but pacman keeps old versions of packages around.

Arch IS tested, using a testing repo, disabled by default. Things go there first if they're liable to break stuff, and there's quite a few people using the testing repo who report issues. Yeah, things do break every once in a while, but I've had similar issues with ubuntu/mint. Only I actually know what the hell is going on in Arch, it doesn't try to hide it from you.

I used to like to tinker with UI's and try to get games running under linux. It's pretty simple to do both now so I've settled on Linux Mint. I don't have much time to tinker anymore. Mint works out of the box and doesn't require much configuration on my end. There is a large community so if I do have issues I can always find an answer.

Mint user here! Here's why:

  • Transparency: I can know exactly what my computer is doing at all times because I can read the source when I'm curious. With Windows, I have no way of knowing what all the system processes are up to. They're all just black boxes. On Linux, if something crashes, I can literally see the exact line of code where it crashed. The last straw for me was when I connected to a wireless network with Wireshark running in the background out of interest. There was all sorts of stuff I didn't like, including requests to Bing by the stupid live-tiles I had forgotten to remove from the start screen.

  • System Architecture I really love the Unix architecture. Path names don't normally contain backslashes, makes programming much nicer. Devices are files rather than hidden away in the kernel somewhere. No registry: everything a program stores are in files somewhere. Better, far less complex file system security. Package management (not really Unix, sue me): Windows doesn't have it. Compilation and development aren't second rate citizens: rather than all the required headers being in C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio 12.0\VC\include, they're in \usr\include. Mounting. Symlinks that don't suck. The list goes on.

  • Security in obscurity Few users, more security! Makes it much tougher for browser 0days to affect me.
Philosophy, package availability, and reliability. It's why I currently use Debian on all of my Linux machines.

My dad was a Solaris admin when I was growing up, my first computer was a Sun UltraSPARC 20. I used Solaris on that machine for a long time, I tried to get many different Linux distros working on it with no success. I finally got Gentoo installed and configured and the rest is history.

Mostly comes down to being better than whatever I was using before in some way. I switched to Linux (Ubuntu back in the Gnome 2 days) because Windows pissed me off by preventing me from fixing a problem I understood. When Unity came out, that motivated me to switch to Kubuntu, and that was nice for a while. Then I got tired for the biannual upgrades and switched to Debian for its rolling release. Rolling release was great, but that lasted all of one release cycle as the feature freeze drove me insane.

I use Sabayon now - it's a Gentoo-derivative with true rolling release and a way more powerful package manager. (Really, the package manager is the biggest difference between distros.) The packages are more up-to-date (about on par with Arch), but you have access to the last 5 or so versions through portage. (The most recent, stable version is available as a binary package, so compile times aren't normally an issue.) The configuration file management is also a lot nicer than in Debian, since it's changes requiring human approval are deferred to the end of the installation/update, instead of stalling it. The only downside is the community is a bit on the small side, but I haven't had any issues getting help on the forums reasonably quickly.

I considered Arch when I was switching, but it seemed like too much work, and it felt like they changed things without enough warning to be suitable for a production machine. e.g. default Python version, /usr/bin - /bin split, etc.
